zh.question: 同一颗恒星从更远处经过黑洞，还会被拉成细长气流吗？
zh.observe: 先比较远近两条路线，再从上方跟踪长尾和回返气流。切到黑洞近景观察橙色亮处；淡线只记录少量物质点最近走过的路径。

academic.title: 拉扯来自引力差
academic.body: 潮汐作用比较的是天体不同位置的引力差，而不是只看中心处引力有多强。当恒星半径 R 远小于中心距离 r 时，中心到近侧的径向差分加速度约为 2GMR/r³。距离缩短会迅速增强这种差异。把它与恒星自身引力比较，可估计潮汐半径 rₜ≈R(M/m)^(1/3)；这只是量级条件，实际破坏还取决于轨道与内部结构。

academic.title: 回返、圆盘化与吸积是不同过程
academic.body: 不同部分获得不同轨道能量和角动量。一些物质可逃离，束缚碎屑则可沿拉长的偏心轨道回返。真实气流相遇和激波可能耗散轨道能量，角动量重新分配影响内移；流动可在一段时间内保持偏心，不保证迅速形成完整圆盘。本页在束缚碎屑外行后转向内行时启用温和耗散，不把回返当成已经求解的碰撞，也不按固定时刻强迫所有物质内移。

academic.title: 亮度、轨迹与观测证据
academic.body: 橙色亮处来自简化耗散造成的轨道能量损失，并会逐渐衰减；它不是温度测量，变暗也不一定表示物质落入。淡线记录少量物质点的最近路径，不是实体环。局部光像另用无自旋薄盘近似计算，不能单凭亮弧证明已形成完整圆盘。真实潮汐瓦解事件需要结合亮度演化、光谱与宿主环境判断；发光物质位于事件视界外，光学暗影与视界也不是同一个边界。

zh.misconception: 黑洞不是把周围一切都吸走的吸尘器；是否碎裂取决于经过距离、轨道和天体结构，发光的通常是视界外的气体。
zh.boundary: 同一批物质点连续展示拉伸、回返与偏心绕行；用渐弱支撑和回返后的耗散作教学近似，没有求解真实碰撞、流体压力、磁场或相对论流体。受热亮度、光学暗影、大小与展示时间不能直接换算成真实事件的温度、吞入量或成盘时间。

narration.label: 先认清主角
narration.text: 我们来跟着一颗恒星旅行。恒星原本是一大团靠自己的引力聚在一起的热气体。旁边的黑洞很特别：越过它的一道边界，连光也不能再逃出来。不过，只是从旁边经过，不一定会掉进去。先看看离得比较远的那条路，恒星能不能继续走。
narration.cue: 显示远距离轨道；等待恒星接近。

narration.label: 近处和远处
narration.text: 现在把经过的路线挪近一些。恒星朝向黑洞的一侧受到的拉力，和另一侧不一样。差别足够大时，恒星就可能被拉散。请暂停一下，找一找：是整颗星一起消失，还是先有一些外层气体离开？给自己一点时间，沿着气流慢慢看。
narration.cue: 切近距离；在外层初次脱离时停顿约四秒。

narration.label: 绕回来，还要继续走
narration.text: 继续播放，原来聚在一起的物质变成了弯弯的长流。有些往远处走，有些走了一段很长的路，又绕回来。回来不等于马上掉进去，也不等于已经变成圆盘。我们从上方跟着它们看：哪一段正在远离，哪一段正在回来？淡淡的线记下少量气体刚走过的路，不是黑洞身旁真的长出了一圈圈环。
narration.cue: 切到俯视；跟随长尾、回返气流与少量最近路径。

narration.label: 亮处为什么会变化
narration.text: 现在切到黑洞近景，找找橙色亮处。真实的气流相遇时可能碰撞、变热。这里用变化的亮光帮助我们想象这个过程，颜色不能告诉我们准确的温度。亮处慢慢变暗，也不一定是气体落进去了。看看那里的气体还在不在，再拉回全景：外面的长尾和弯弯的气流，仍然在继续旅行。
narration.cue: 切近景观察局部亮处与衰减，再回俯视比较气体仍在的位置。

en.question: Would the same star become a long stream if it passed farther from the black hole?
en.observe: Compare distant and close passes, then track the tail and returning streams from above. Use the black hole close-up to inspect orange patches; faint lines record only a few parcels’ recent paths.

academic.title: Tides measure a difference
academic.body: Tides compare gravity at different positions within an object, rather than just its central acceleration. For stellar radius R much smaller than distance r, the radial acceleration difference from the center to the near side is approximately 2GMR/r³. Comparing this with the star’s self-gravity gives the order-of-magnitude tidal radius rₜ≈R(M/m)^(1/3). Orbit and internal structure affect the actual outcome.

academic.title: Fallback, circularization and accretion are distinct
academic.body: Different parts acquire different orbital energies and angular momenta. Some can escape, while bound debris can return on elongated, eccentric orbits. Stream interactions and shocks may dissipate orbital energy, and angular-momentum redistribution affects inward motion. The flow may remain eccentric instead of quickly forming a complete disk. Here, gentle dissipation starts after bound debris turns inward following outward motion. A return is not a solved collision, and no fixed time forces all material inward.

academic.title: Brightness, paths and observational evidence
academic.body: Orange patches follow orbital-energy loss from simplified dissipation and gradually fade. They are not temperature measurements, and fading does not necessarily mean capture. Faint lines trace a few parcels’ recent paths, not solid rings. A separate non-spinning thin-disk approximation produces the local optical image; a bright arc alone does not establish a complete disk. Real tidal disruptions are assessed using changing brightness, spectra and the host environment. Emission comes from outside the horizon, which is not identical to the optical shadow.

en.misconception: A black hole does not vacuum up everything nearby. Distance, orbit, and internal structure affect disruption; the glowing gas is outside the horizon.
en.boundary: One continuous material population illustrates stretching, return and eccentric motion. Weakening support and dissipation after return are teaching approximations, without physical collisions, gas pressure, magnetic fields or relativistic fluid dynamics. Heating brightness, optical shadow, sizes and playback time cannot yield a real event’s temperature, captured mass or disk-formation time.

narration.label: Meet the travelers
narration.text: Let’s travel with a star. A star is a huge ball of hot gas held together by its own gravity. The black hole nearby has a special boundary: once something crosses it inward, even light cannot escape. But passing nearby does not always mean falling in. First watch the farther route and see whether the star continues on its way.
narration.cue: Show the distant pass and wait for approach.

narration.label: Different pulls
narration.text: Now bring the route closer. The side facing the black hole feels a different pull from the far side. A large enough difference can pull the star apart. Pause for a moment. Does the whole star vanish together, or do some outer layers leave first? Take your time and follow the flowing material.
narration.cue: Pause for about four seconds when outer layers first detach.

narration.label: Returning is another part of the journey
narration.text: Keep watching as the material becomes a long, curved stream. Some travels away. Some takes a long route and comes back. Returning does not mean falling straight in or already becoming a disk. Follow the streams from above: which part is moving away, and which is returning? Faint lines mark the recent paths of a few gas parcels. They are not real rings growing around the black hole.
narration.cue: Use the top view; follow the tail, returning streams and selected recent paths.

narration.label: Why the bright patches change
narration.text: Use the black hole close-up and find the orange patches. Real streams may collide and heat up when they meet. The changing glow helps us imagine this process, but its colors cannot tell us an exact temperature. A fading patch does not always mean the gas has fallen in. Check whether the gas is still there, then return to the overview: the long tail and curved streams are continuing their journey outside.
narration.cue: Inspect local patches and fading in the close-up, then use the top view to locate the remaining gas.
